newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Nato ministers lay groundwork for expansion east.
newsitem.headline: Nato ministers lay groundwork for expansion east.

text.p: Hailing the creation of a new European security order, NATO begins laying the groundwork this week for expanding eastward into territory once ruled by its old Cold War foe, the Warsaw Pact.

Foreign ministers who make up NATO's North Atlantic Council will meet at a luxury resort outside Lisbon on Thursday, two days after Russian and alliance leaders signed a landmark cooperation treaty in Paris.

The summit at France's Elysee Palace was staged for maximum international exposure, with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, U.S. President Bill Clinton and other heads of state joining together in an elaborate show of good will.

It clears the way for NATO ministers to begin hammering out plans to extend membership to former Soviet-bloc nations -- a move Russia had bitterly opposed but ultimately admitted it was powerless to stop.
"The Sintra meeting will help us put the Cold War behind us," a NATO diplomat said. "It's where we start dealing with the nuts-and-bolts decisions of building a new European defence."

Meeting behind closed doors, ministers are expected to agree on a plan to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- the post-communist nations that have evolved most rapidly toward democracy and market economies -- to join at a July 8-9 summit in Madrid, NATO sources said.
That would give the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the guarantor of western European defence for five decades, its first foothold behind what was once called the "Iron Curtain".

Other former members of the Warsaw Pact, the now-disbanded military alliance maintained by the old Soviet Union as a counter-threat to NATO, are also pressing for entry but will probably be told to wait, officials said.
Underlying the drive for NATO membership is the fear that Russia might some day abandon democratic reforms and threaten eastern Europe again, U.S. officials acknowledge privately.
Mindful of the diplomatic sensitivities, NATO ministers are unlikely to make any public announcements about membership decisions during the two-day Sintra meeting.

Russia, which has called expansion of the 16-member alliance a "strategic mistake", has warned that any attempt to take in former Soviet republics such as Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia would be unacceptable.

But a NATO spokesman insisted that the Baltic states, which won their independence when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, would remain eligible for membership. Despite such assurances, a NATO diplomat said privately it was "unrealistic" to think the Baltics would be admitted any time soon.

As a consolation prize, countries excluded from the first round of NATO enlargement will be invited to forge closer military and political ties to the alliance through a strengthened "Partnership for Peace," officials said.

NATO ministers expect to finalize the details on Friday when they meet more than 20 foreign ministers from eastern Europe and former Soviet republics now participating in cooperation programs. The new grouping will be named the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.

Russia had strongly opposed NATO enlargement as a threat to its own security. But from the start of negotiations, NATO officials left no doubt that expansion would go ahead whether Russia liked it or not.
The outcome was the signing of the Russia-NATO "Founding Act," a historic agreement that redefined the European security order while seeking to ease Moscow's fears.
Yeltsin won assurances the allies have no plans to deploy nuclear weapons or troops on the soil of new members, and Russia was granted a voice, but not a veto, in NATO decisions.
Now that expansion is all but guaranteed, the most heated debate among NATO foreign minister gathering in Sintra may center on who pays the bill, a Spanish government official said.
Cost estimates for bringing eastern Europe under the NATO umbrella run from a low of $35 billion to a high of over $100 billion up to 2009.
